claims.text: The starting catalyst is a near-equiatomic Cu–Ni–Co–Fe–Pd multi-principal-element alloy with a homogeneous metallic surface.
Mild oxidation in an oxygen-lean environment at 150–200 °C can form a thin high-entropy oxide shell on the alloy catalyst.
The oxidation-created shell will contain abundant oxygen vacancies.
The oxide shell will form uniformly on particle exteriors.
The oxide shell modifies the catalyst's surface electronic structure.
The modified electronic structure lowers the activation energy for CO oxidation.
The modified electronic structure lowers the activation energy for hydrocarbon oxidation.
Oxygen vacancies facilitate dynamic adsorbate exchange.
Vacancy-mediated adsorbate exchange reduces the binding strength of H2O and NO poisoning species.
The oxide shell acts as a physical barrier to catalyst-particle sintering.
The oxidation-treated catalyst will have lower CO and hydrocarbon light-off temperatures than the untreated catalyst, with light-off below 150 °C.
The oxidation-treated catalyst will resist H2O and NO poisoning better than the untreated catalyst.
The oxidation-treated catalyst will have improved structural stability during extended thermal cycling.
Automotive exhaust operation involves frequent temperature fluctuations that motivate cyclic thermal testing.
The benefits will persist during transient, below-150 °C exposure to CO, hydrocarbons, H2O, and NO.
The benefits will persist under cyclic aging conditions representative of automotive operation.
Excessive oxidation can create a thick or insulating oxide layer that reduces catalytic activity.
The untreated multi-principal-element catalyst does not achieve the required combined activity, poison resistance, and durability under realistic exhaust conditions.
The magnitude of the performance improvement depends on oxidation time, temperature, and oxygen partial pressure.

contradictions.description: The boundary and uncertainty fields predict that excessive oxidation lies outside the beneficial treatment window and may degrade activity, whereas the falsification rule treats degradation caused by excessive oxidation as falsifying the mild, controlled-oxidation hypothesis. Failure under an explicitly excluded treatment regime would not by itself falsify the core hypothesis.
